C005.subject: intermittent fasting with structured behavioral support
C005.object: long-term dietary adherence compared to intermittent fasting alone or daily caloric restriction
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: intermittent fasting with structured behavioral support long-term dietary adherence compared to intermittent fasting alone or daily caloric restriction]

[PATH:empirical] Randomized controlled trial comparing intermittent fasting with structured behavioral support (e.g., cognitive-behavioral therapy, dietary counseling) vs. intermittent fasting alone vs. daily caloric restriction, with adherence measured via self-report and objective biomarkers at 6, 12, and 18 months in a US-based overweight adult population. — Directly tests the hypothesis by comparing the three conditions in the specified population and time frame, providing causal evidence on long-term adherence.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of behavioral interventions (e.g., counseling, self-monitoring, social support) combined with dietary regimens (including intermittent fasting) on dietary adherence outcomes in overweight adults, focusing on studies with follow-up >6 months. — Synthesizes existing evidence to assess whether structured behavioral support consistently improves adherence over dietary regimens alone, and identifies effect sizes and moderators.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical framework from self-determination theory and habit formation models applied to dietary adherence in intermittent fasting, with testable predictions about intrinsic motivation and automaticity as mediators. — Provides mechanistic understanding of why structured support might enhance long-term adherence, guiding the design of future empirical tests and identifying key variables to measure.

C006.subject: intermittent fasting
C006.object: long-term dietary adherence compared to daily caloric restriction
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: intermittent fasting long-term dietary adherence compared to daily caloric restriction]

[PATH:empirical] Long-term randomized controlled trials comparing intermittent fasting (e.g., 5:2 diet, time-restricted eating) vs. continuous caloric restriction on adherence metrics (dropout rates, self-reported compliance) at 12 months in overweight adults from US and Western European cohorts. — Direct empirical comparison in the target population and timeframe would provide highest-quality evidence to confirm or refute the hypothesized difference in adherence.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of behavioral adherence in dietary interventions, focusing on dropout rates and self-monitoring compliance in intermittent fasting vs. daily restriction protocols across multiple studies. — Synthesizing existing data can reveal consistent patterns and effect sizes, addressing the disputed status with broader statistical power.

[PATH:theoretical] Behavioral economics and psychological models of habit formation and reward processing applied to intermittent fasting vs. daily restriction, examining factors like dietary flexibility, social constraints, and craving dynamics over 12 months. — Theoretical analysis can identify mechanisms (e.g., reduced decision fatigue vs. increased hunger during fasting windows) that predict adherence differences, guiding interpretation of empirical findings.

C007.subject: intermittent fasting with early time-restricted feeding (eTRF)
C007.object: superior improvement in 24-hour glucose variability compared to matched caloric restriction with later eating windows
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: intermittent fasting with early time-restricted feeding (eTRF) superior improvement in 24-hour glucose variability compared to matched caloric restriction with later eating windows]

[PATH:empirical] Randomized controlled trial comparing eTRF (e.g., 8-hour eating window ending before 3 PM) vs. isocaloric later eating window (e.g., 12-hour window ending at 8 PM) in non-diabetic adults with overweight or obesity, with continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) for 24-hour glucose variability metrics (e.g., MAGE, CV%) over at least 2 weeks. — Directly tests the hypothesis by isolating meal timing from caloric intake, using gold-standard CGM data to assess glucose variability differences.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of time-restricted feeding studies that report glucose variability outcomes, stratified by eating window timing and caloric matching, with subgroup analysis on non-diabetic overweight/obese populations. — Synthesizes existing evidence to determine if eTRF consistently shows superior glucose variability reduction compared to later windows, controlling for confounders like total energy intake.

[PATH:empirical] Mechanistic study examining circadian clock gene expression (e.g., PER, CRY) and insulin sensitivity in adipose or muscle tissue under eTRF vs. later eating schedules, using a crossover design in non-diabetic adults. — Provides biological plausibility by testing whether early feeding aligns with circadian rhythms to improve glucose regulation, explaining potential superiority in variability outcomes.

scope.domain: glycemic control in non-diabetic adults with overweight or obesity

qualifier.tension: Prior studies did not control for meal timing independently of caloric intake; this hypothesis isolates the circadian timing effect.

C008.subject: caloric restriction alone
C008.object: equivalent metabolic advantages (e.g., improved insulin sensitivity) as intermittent fasting
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: caloric restriction alone equivalent metabolic advantages (e.g., improved insulin sensitivity) as intermittent fasting]

[PATH:empirical] Head-to-head randomized controlled trial comparing caloric restriction alone vs. intermittent fasting (e.g., 5:2 or time-restricted eating) with matched total caloric intake, measuring insulin sensitivity via hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp in non-diabetic adults. — Directly tests equivalence of metabolic advantages by controlling for caloric intake, reducing confounding from weight loss differences; clamp method is gold standard for insulin sensitivity.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of studies up to 2023 that compare caloric restriction and intermittent fasting on insulin sensitivity and other metabolic markers, with subgroup analysis by total caloric deficit and study duration. — Aggregates existing evidence to assess overall effect size and heterogeneity; can reveal if equivalence holds across populations and protocols, addressing the disputed status.

[PATH:empirical] Long-term observational cohort study tracking metabolic health outcomes (e.g., HbA1c, fasting insulin, HOMA-IR) in non-diabetic individuals who self-select caloric restriction or intermittent fasting, with statistical adjustment for caloric intake and physical activity. — Provides real-world data on sustained effects beyond controlled trial durations; helps evaluate if equivalence persists under typical adherence and lifestyle conditions.

scope.domain: metabolic health markers in non-diabetic populations

qualifier.geographic: global, predominantly Western and Asian clinical trial populations

C009.subject: intermittent fasting
C009.object: anticipatory overeating prior to fasting windows than by post-fast compensatory overeating
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: intermittent fasting anticipatory overeating prior to fasting windows than by post-fast compensatory overeating]

[PATH:empirical] Ecological momentary assessment (EMA) studies tracking real-time eating behavior and appetite ratings before and after fasting windows in intermittent fasting practitioners — EMA can capture anticipatory overeating in natural settings, providing direct evidence of its prevalence and magnitude compared to post-fast compensatory eating, which is crucial for testing the hypothesis.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) on intermittent fasting that report pre-fast and post-fast caloric intake data in free-living participants — A synthesis of existing RCTs with dietary recall or food diary data can quantify the relative contribution of anticipatory versus compensatory overeating to overall energy intake, offering confirmatory or refuting evidence across studies.

[PATH:empirical] Experimental laboratory study comparing ad libitum energy intake during a pre-fast period versus a post-fast period under controlled conditions, with manipulation of fasting window duration — Controlled experiments can isolate the causal effect of anticipated fasting on pre-fast eating behavior, reducing confounds present in observational studies and providing mechanistic evidence for the hypothesis.

scope.domain: real-world eating patterns in free-living individuals

qualifier.geographic: global, primarily Western and urban populations

C010.subject: compensatory behaviors
C010.object: psychological and physiological adaptations that support sustained caloric deficit
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: compensatory behaviors psychological and physiological adaptations that support sustained caloric deficit]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal cohort studies (e.g., NHANES or UK Biobank) tracking self-reported compensatory behaviors (e.g., dietary lapses, exercise reduction) alongside physiological markers (e.g., resting metabolic rate, ghrelin levels) over 6+ months in free-living individuals with caloric deficits. — Directly tests whether compensatory behaviors are counteracted by physiological adaptations in real-world settings, addressing the temporal and geographic scope.

[PATH:empirical] Controlled experimental trials (e.g., randomized controlled trials with isocaloric vs. deficit diets) measuring both behavioral compensation (e.g., food intake logs, activity monitors) and physiological adaptations (e.g., metabolic slowing, hormone changes) over periods >6 months. — Provides causal evidence for the interplay between behavioral and physiological mechanisms, with high internal validity to confirm or refute the hypothesis.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analyses of weight loss maintenance studies (e.g., from the National Weight Control Registry) examining the prevalence and impact of compensatory behaviors on sustained caloric deficit. — Synthesizes existing evidence to assess the overall effect size and consistency of the hypothesized counteraction, leveraging large-scale observational data.

scope.domain: real-world eating patterns in free-living individuals

qualifier.geographic: primarily in high-income countries with abundant food availability
